The paper writes the two loops formally in Section 3.2 on page 2. The text layer loses most of the math symbols, so I read the equations from the PDF page images.

**Inner loop (task-specific prompt update)**, p. 2:

  θᵢ′ = θ − α ∇_θ L_{Tᵢ}(f_θ ; Dᵢ^support)

- θ ∈ ℝ^{l×d} is the soft-prompt initialization. Here l is the prompt length and d is the LLM's embedding dimension (p. 2).
- α is the inner-loop learning rate. f_θ is the LLM conditioned on the prompt θ (p. 2).
- **Data split: the support set Dᵢ^support** of user task Tᵢ.

**Outer loop (meta-objective across tasks)**, p. 2:

  min_θ Σᵢ L_{Tᵢ}(f_{θᵢ′} ; Dᵢ^query)

- The loss uses the adapted prompt θᵢ′ and is summed over the sampled user tasks. The minimization is over the shared initialization θ (p. 2).
- **Data split: the query set Dᵢ^query** of each task.

**How the splits are defined:**
- Each user is one task Tᵢ ~ p(T). Their interactions Dᵢ = {(x_k, y_k)}_{k=1}^K are divided into a support set and a query set. The goal is a θ that, after a few updates on Dᵢ^support, gives low loss on Dᵢ^query (pp. 1–2).
- During episodic training, each user has 1–5 interactions in the support set and 1–5 in the query set (p. 2, §3.4).
- At test time, each user has a support set of K ∈ {1, 3, 5} interactions (p. 3). Most experiments use K = 5 (p. 3).
- Gradients only update the soft prompt P, which is placed in front of the input as [P; X]. The LLM itself stays frozen (p. 2, §3.3).

The introduction gives a shorter version on p. 1: θᵢ′ = θ − α∇_θ L_{Tᵢ}(θ) and min_θ Σᵢ L_{Tᵢ}(θᵢ′). It leaves the splits out of the formulas, but the surrounding text says adaptation uses D_support and the aim is the best performance on D_query.

The paper also uses Reptile, a first-order alternative to MAML. Reptile follows the same episodic structure and avoids second-order gradients, but sometimes loses some accuracy (p. 2, §3.5).
